title: Quantum Stochastic Walks on the Permutation Group
authors: Feng He, Arthur Hutsalyuk, Giuseppe Mussardo, Andrea Stampiggi
abstract: How rapidly does order give way to randomness, and can quantum coherence accelerate this process? We address these questions through the paradigmatic problem of card shuffling, formulated as a random walk on the symmetric group $S_n$. We first recast the random-transposition walk studied by Diaconis and Shahshahani, as well as more general walks generated by conjugacy classes of $S_n$, in continuous time. We then identify the transition matrix of each classical walk with a permutation Hamiltonian generating a corresponding unitary quantum walk. Purely unitary evolution, however, does not generically converge to the uniform distribution in the classical sense of mixing: coherence preserves information rather than erasing it. We therefore embed the problem into a quantum stochastic walk, where coherent dynamics competes with the dissipative process responsible for classical mixing. In this setting, quantum coherence assists randomization. We prove that it can only decrease the distance from the uniform distribution in the computational basis and can therefore accelerate mixing. An analysis of the slowest mode yields a criterion for the coupling strength required to produce an appreciable speedup. Finally, numerical results reveal a scaling collapse of the ratio between quantum and classical mixing times onto a simple one-parameter form. Our results illustrate how coherence and dissipation can cooperate in the emergence of randomness in walks on permutation groups.
summary: This paper analyzes the mixing dynamics of random walks on the symmetric group by comparing classical and quantum stochastic processes. It demonstrates that quantum coherence can actively assist the randomization process, accelerating the rate at which the system approaches a uniform, mixed state. The findings establish a framework for understanding how coherence and dissipation cooperate in physical systems.
main_problem: The paper investigates how quantum coherence affects the rate at which order gives way to randomness (mixing) in systems modeled by random walks on the symmetric group $S_n$. It compares quantum stochastic walks to classical random walks.
main_result: While coherence does not accelerate the convergence of the full density matrix to equilibrium, it can accelerate the mixing of the measurement probabilities, demonstrating a cooperation between coherence and dissipation.
method: The authors use continuous-time random walk formulations, comparing unitary quantum evolution with dissipative quantum stochastic walks (QSWs) governed by Lindblad dynamics.
model_or_system: The model is the random walk on the symmetric group $S_n$, specifically using random transpositions or random $q$-cycles. The dynamics are analyzed via both classical Markov chains and quantum stochastic processes.
key_observables: Mixing time (classical and quantum), Total-variation distance ($D_\alpha(t)$), Trace distance, and the Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR).
important_parameters: The coupling strength ($\alpha$), the size of the group ($n$), and the cycle length ($q$).
main_assumptions: The enhanced mixing result is guaranteed only due to the specific algebraic structure where the dissipative dynamics and coherent dynamics commute.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the evolution of the total variation distance during the transition from ordered to random phases, and show a scaling collapse of the ratio between quantum and classical mixing times.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by recasting classical random walks into continuous time, analyzing the unitary quantum walk, and finally embedding the problem into a QSW to study the interplay between coherent evolution and dissipation.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, mathematically rigorous example of how environmental coupling (dissipation) can interact with quantum coherence to enhance the rate of thermalization or randomization, which is highly relevant for open quantum systems.
